items.title: Explore → Plan → Code → Commit
items.summary: The four-beat prompt that fixes most 'it just started editing things' complaints.
items.detail:
The failure mode of a coding agent is starting to type before it understands. This prompt forces reading before planning and planning before editing, with an approval gate you control.

Use it for anything touching more than two files.
items.snippet:
Read the files relevant to [task] but do NOT write any code yet.

Now think hard and give me a plan: what changes, in which files, in what order, and what could break.

[you approve]

Implement the plan. Verify as you go. Then commit with a message explaining the why.

items.title: Tests first, and don't you dare mock it
items.summary: Explicitly forbid the shortcut and TDD actually works with an agent.
items.detail: Without the 'do not write an implementation' clause you get tests and code written together, which means the tests are shaped to pass rather than to specify. The second clause — don't modify the tests — stops the agent from 'fixing' a failure by weakening the assertion.
items.snippet:
Write tests for [behaviour] from these input/output pairs. The implementation does NOT exist yet — do not write it, do not mock it. Run the tests and confirm they fail for the right reason.

---

Now implement until every test passes. Do not modify any test file. If a test looks wrong, stop and tell me instead of changing it.

items.title: Root cause, not symptom
items.summary: Force a timeline and three hypotheses before it's allowed to propose a fix.
items.detail: Agents pattern-match to the first plausible cause and then rationalise. Asking for ranked hypotheses with disconfirming evidence gets you an actual investigation — and often reveals that the obvious cause was wrong.
items.snippet:
Here is the failure: [paste error/log].

Before proposing any fix: build a timeline of what happened, then give me three candidate root causes ranked by evidence, and for each one say what evidence would rule it OUT. Then tell me which single check would discriminate between them fastest.

items.title: Correctness-only review
items.summary: Demand a failure scenario per finding and the style noise disappears.
items.detail: An open 'review this' prompt returns nitpicks because nitpicks are easy. Requiring concrete breaking inputs for every finding filters out everything the reviewer can't actually justify.
items.snippet:
Review this diff for correctness bugs only — no style, no naming, no preferences.

For each finding give exactly: file:line · the defect in one sentence · concrete inputs or state that produce the wrong result. If you cannot state a failing scenario, do not report it.

items.title: Give me the tour
items.summary: The first prompt in any unfamiliar repo, after /init.
items.detail: Asking for a narrative path through the code beats asking for a summary: it forces real file references and exposes the seams where the architecture doesn't match the folder names.
items.snippet: I'm new to this codebase. Trace one full [request / job / user action] from entry point to persistence, naming every file it passes through and what each one is responsible for. Then tell me the three places where the structure surprised you.

items.title: Stay in your lane
items.summary: The clause that stops a small fix turning into a 40-file diff.
items.detail: Agents are enthusiastic refactorers. Bounding the blast radius explicitly — and asking for out-of-scope observations as a list rather than as edits — gives you the insight without the diff.
items.snippet:
Fix only [specific issue]. Do not refactor, rename, reformat or 'improve' anything else, even if it's clearly wrong.

If you notice other problems, list them at the end as suggestions — don't act on them.

items.title: Write it like the neighbours
items.summary: Point at an exemplar file instead of describing your conventions.
items.detail: Style instructions in prose are vague; a reference file is unambiguous. This is also the fix for an agent that keeps writing comments your codebase doesn't have.
items.snippet: src/services/billing.ts is exactly the style we want — error handling, naming, comment density, test layout. Write the new [thing] so a reviewer couldn't tell which of the two files was written by a human.

items.title: Ultrathink the design decision
items.summary: Buy reasoning where it pays: irreversible architectural choices.
items.detail: Asking for the trade-offs and a recommendation — rather than a survey — is what turns a long think into a decision you can act on. Demanding the failure mode of the recommended option is what stops it being a sales pitch.
items.snippet: Ultrathink this: we need [outcome] under [constraints]. Give me two or three viable designs, the real trade-off between them, your recommendation, and — specifically — how your recommended option fails and how we'd know early.

items.title: Verify before you tell me you're done
items.summary: Make 'done' mean something by defining the check up front.
items.detail: 'It should work now' is the most expensive sentence in agent-assisted coding. Naming the verification command in the prompt turns completion into an observable event rather than a claim.
items.snippet: When you believe you're finished, run [npm test && npm run typecheck] and paste the real output. If anything fails, keep going — do not report success with failing checks, and don't tell me it 'should' work.

items.title: Commit message from the diff
items.summary: It has read every line of the change. You have read three.
items.detail: Works best staged: the agent sees exactly what's going in. Add your house rules to CLAUDE.md once (conventional commits, ticket prefix, no attribution trailers) and drop this prompt to a single line forever after.
items.snippet: Read the staged diff and write the commit message. Conventional-commit subject under 72 chars; body explains why this change exists, not what the lines do. No attribution trailers.

items.title: Interrogate me before you build
items.summary: Flip the direction — make it ask the questions a good engineer would.
items.detail: Half of bad output is a half-specified request. Asking for the questions first surfaces the decisions you hadn't made, before they're baked into code you have to review.
items.snippet: Before you write anything: ask me the five questions whose answers would most change how you'd build [feature]. Wait for my answers. Then plan.

items.title: Tell me what you're unsure about
items.summary: A closing clause that turns confident-sounding output into reviewable output.
items.detail: Appended to any substantial task, this separates what the agent verified from what it assumed. The assumptions list is where your review time should go — and it's usually short.
items.snippet: At the end, add two short lists: (1) what you actually verified by running or reading, and (2) what you assumed without checking. Be specific and don't pad either list.
